```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# The corpus is bundled with the suggested sbert package. Without it the
# vignette shows code and prose only.
has_sbert <- requireNamespace("sbert", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE, eval = has_sbert,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%")
library(hypergraphs)
```

This tutorial analyses the document structure of a bibliographic corpus
using a word-based hypergraph. Documents are nodes, and words are hyperedges
linking the documents in which they occur. Spectral clustering partitions
the documents according to this structure. Keywords, coherence measures,
and representative abstracts are then used to interpret the clusters;
the algorithm does not assign substantive topic meanings on its own.

The example uses the `covid` dataset distributed with sbert, containing
`r format(nrow(sbert::covid), big.mark = ",")` Scopus records on COVID-19
and education published between 2020 and 2024. The analysis retains the
abstract text and publication year for preprocessing and interpretation.

## Text cleaning

Bibliographic abstracts can contain HTML, citation markers, identifiers,
and publisher notices. `clean_text()` applies a defined set of text
transformations: it decodes HTML entities, removes tags and selected
non-content strings, and standardises typographic characters. It preserves
the input row alignment. Text with an alphabetic-character share below
`min_content` becomes an empty string. The additional `remove` pattern
below removes Scopus's missing-abstract placeholder.

```{r clean}
abstracts <- clean_text(sbert::covid, column = "Abstract",
                        remove = "no abstract available", min_content = 0.5)
abstracts <- unique(abstracts)
```

```{r clean-values, include = FALSE}
n_placeholder <- sum(grepl("no abstract available", sbert::covid$Abstract,
                           ignore.case = TRUE))
n_unique <- nrow(abstracts)
n_empty <- sum(!nzchar(abstracts$Abstract))
```

Cleaning identifies `r n_placeholder` missing-abstract placeholders.
After removal of duplicate records, there are
`r format(n_unique, big.mark = ",")` records, including `r n_empty` empty
abstracts. Keeping these rows during cleaning preserves the alignment
between text and publication year. The hypergraph constructor subsequently
excludes documents without retained tokens.

## Hypergraph construction

With `construction = "bag"` and `nodes = "doc"`, each abstract is a
node and each retained word is a hyperedge. The default `weight = "n"`
stores the word count in each document–word incidence cell. Tokenisation
uses lower-case alphabetic strings. Repeated words contribute to the cell
count, while word order is discarded. Documents without any retained token
are excluded with a warning.

```{r build}
stops <- c(stop_words_en(), "covid", "pandemic")
hg <- text_hypergraph(abstracts, column = "Abstract", stop_words = stops,
                      min_count = 5L)
hg
```

The stop list combines common English words with `covid` and
`pandemic`, which define the corpus subject and are removed by an explicit
analytical choice. `min_count = 5` retains words with at least five
occurrences across the corpus. The default storage rule uses a sparse
incidence matrix when the number of document–word cells reaches one
million; unobserved memberships are then not stored explicitly.

## Number of topics

The spectrum of the normalised hypergraph Laplacian provides a
diagnostic for choosing a clustering resolution (Zhou et al. 2006).
`what = "eigenvalues"` returns the smallest eigenvalues and the gap after
each. A relatively large gap after the kth eigenvalue is a heuristic for
considering k clusters. It is not a statistical test or a unique estimate
of the number of topics. The first gap concerns separation from the
zero eigenvalue and is excluded from the comparison below.

```{r count}
spectrum <- hg_cluster(hg, k = 18, seed = 1, what = "eigenvalues")
spectrum
```

```{r count-values, include = FALSE}
informative <- subset(spectrum, index >= 2 & !is.na(gap))
ranked_gaps <- informative[order(-informative$gap), ]
best_k <- ranked_gaps$index[1:2]
```

Among the inspected nontrivial gaps, the largest occur after indices
`r best_k[1]` and `r best_k[2]`, with values
`r sprintf("%.4f", ranked_gaps$gap[1])` and
`r sprintf("%.4f", ranked_gaps$gap[2])`. These resolutions are candidates
for further inspection. The example instead uses 16 clusters to match
the number of topics in the published analysis of Saqr et al. (2023).
Using the same number permits a descriptive comparison; it does not
reproduce that topic model or validate the 16-cluster solution.

## Partition

`hg_cluster()` embeds the documents in eigenvectors associated with
the smallest Laplacian eigenvalues and applies k-means to that embedding.
The default `type = "zhou"` uses binary hyperedge membership and unit
hyperedge weights for this object. The stored term counts therefore do
not determine this particular clustering. The returned table contains
one cluster label per document. Set `seed` to reproduce the k-means fit.

```{r cut}
topics <- hg_cluster(hg, k = 16, seed = 1)
head(topics)
```

## Topic description

Use `hg_keywords()` to describe each cluster's vocabulary. The returned
table contains one row per cluster and word, with the selected score,
the proportion of the word's corpus count assigned to the cluster, and
the number of cluster documents containing it. The default mass score
sums incidence weights within a cluster. With count-weighted incidence,
this is the word's total count in the cluster.

```{r name-default}
hg_keywords(hg, topics)
```

The default ranking emphasises common terms such as learning,
students, education, online, and teaching. To inspect more concentrated
vocabulary, rank by `share`, the fraction of each word's corpus count
occurring in the cluster. This is a word-level concentration measure,
not the proportion of cluster documents containing the word. The
`min_docs` threshold excludes words with insufficient document support.
Several scoring methods can be requested together for comparison.

```{r name-owned}
words <- hg_keywords(hg, topics, type = c("frequency", "ctfidf", "centrality"),
                     sort_by = "share", min_docs = 15)
words
```

The three requested scores are within-cluster frequency,
class-based tf-idf (`ctfidf`; Grootendorst 2022), and centrality in the
cluster's word hypergraph. PageRank is the default centrality for this
keyword calculation. Because the table is sorted by `share`, that column
governs the primary ranking even when several scores are requested.
Inspect the keywords alongside sample abstracts before assigning topic
names. A keyword list alone does not establish that a cluster represents
a single, coherent literature.

The keyword plot displays one panel per cluster and scoring method.
Compare both the ranking and the underlying document support.

```{r name-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 40}
plot(words, value = "share")
```

## Topic sizes

`hg_topic_sizes()` returns the number and proportion of documents
assigned to each cluster. Its optional `weights` argument takes a numeric
vector named by document identifier, permitting summaries weighted by
quantities such as citation count. Weighted shares describe that chosen
quantity and have a different denominator from document shares.

```{r sizes, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
sizes <- hg_topic_sizes(hg, topics)
sizes
plot(sizes)
```

## Topic coherence and exclusivity

`hg_topic_quality()` evaluates the most probable words of each cluster
using coherence and exclusivity measures also used in topic-model analysis
(Roberts et al. 2019). These measures support a comparison when the corpus,
vocabulary, number of top words, and scoring conventions are held fixed.

UMass coherence evaluates document co-occurrence for pairs of top-ranked
words (Mimno et al. 2011). The implementation follows the smoothing
convention used by `stm`: it adds 0.01 to both the joint document count
and the document count of the earlier-ranked word, then sums the logarithms
of their ratios. The score is nonpositive. Values nearer zero indicate
stronger co-occurrence among the selected words.

FREX combines frequency and exclusivity ranks through a weighted harmonic
mean (Bischof and Airoldi 2012). The topic summary sums these values over
the selected top words. A larger value favours words that are both
relatively frequent within the topic and concentrated in that topic.

```{r quality, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
quality <- hg_topic_quality(hg, topics, min_docs = 15)
quality
plot(quality)
```

Read the two measures together and inspect individual documents.
High coherence and exclusivity indicate a concentrated, co-occurring
vocabulary under these definitions, but do not establish thematic validity.
Low coherence can indicate heterogeneous content, sparse occurrence, or
preprocessing effects. `coherence = "npmi"` selects normalised pointwise
mutual information; `words =` supplies word lists from another model.

## Soft membership

`hg_membership()` provides a graded description of the hard partition
in the spectral embedding. It computes each cluster centre as the mean
of its document positions, then assigns weights proportional to inverse
squared distance and normalises them over clusters. This uses the fuzzy
c-means weighting formula with fuzziness two (Bezdek 1981), with the
partition centres held fixed. Coincident centres share the weight equally.
These are geometric membership weights, not estimated topic probabilities.

```{r membership, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
membership <- hg_membership(hg, topics)
head(membership, 16)
plot(membership)
```

```{r membership-values, include = FALSE}
uniform <- 1 / 16
own <- subset(membership, cluster == topic)$membership
first_doc <- subset(membership, node == "doc_1")
first_m <- setNames(first_doc$membership, first_doc$topic)
distance_ratio <- function(a, b) sqrt(first_m[[a]] / first_m[[b]])
ranked_m <- tapply(membership$membership, membership$node,
                   \(m) sort(m, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2])
closeness <- vapply(ranked_m, \(m) 1 - sqrt(m[2] / m[1]), numeric(1))
```

Membership weights sum to one for each document. With 16 clusters,
the equal-weight reference is `r uniform`. The median weight assigned to a
document's hard cluster is `r sprintf("%.2f", median(own))`, or
`r sprintf("%.1f", median(own) / uniform)` times that reference.
For inverse-squared-distance weights, the square root of a membership
ratio equals the inverse ratio of the corresponding distances. For the
first document, the distance to Cluster 2 relative to Cluster 1 is
`r sprintf("%.1f", distance_ratio("Cluster 1", "Cluster 2"))`, and the
ratio for Cluster 3 is
`r sprintf("%.1f", distance_ratio("Cluster 1", "Cluster 3"))`.
The median relative separation between the nearest and second-nearest
centres is `r round(100 * median(closeness))`%. These results describe
separation in the chosen embedding, not certainty about substantive
topic membership. The boxplots show the distribution of weights assigned
to each cluster by its own documents.

## Relations between topics

`topic_network()` compares clusters through their retained vocabulary.
For each cluster, form a vector giving the number of documents containing
each word. The unnormalised relation between two clusters is the dot
product of these vectors. With `similarity = "cosine"`, the relation is
divided by the product of their vector norms. The result describes
vocabulary similarity and ranges from zero to one for these nonnegative
vectors. `what = "network"` returns an object for network plotting.

```{r relations}
relations <- topic_network(hg, clusters = topics, similarity = "cosine")
head(relations)
```

```{r relations-values, include = FALSE}
all_relations <- topic_network(hg, clusters = topics, similarity = "cosine")
upper_quartile <- unname(quantile(all_relations$weight, 0.75))
```

The `r nrow(all_relations)` reported similarities range from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(all_relations$weight))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(all_relations$weight))`. The figure retains edges
at or above the upper quartile, `r sprintf("%.2f", upper_quartile)`.
Line width represents similarity. The spring layout provides a visual
arrangement of these relations; plotted distances are not the cosine
similarities themselves.

```{r relations-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7}
network <- topic_network(hg, clusters = topics, similarity = "cosine",
                         what = "network")
cograph::splot(network, layout = "spring", minimum = upper_quartile,
               edge_width_range = c(0.5, 8))
```

## Summary

The analysis partitions `r format(hg$n_nodes, big.mark = ",")` abstracts
into 16 clusters and describes them using vocabulary, sizes, and graded
memberships. The eigenvalue diagnostic identifies other candidate
resolutions, while 16 was chosen for comparison with a published topic
analysis. These are distinct reasons for choosing a cluster count.

Before using a partition substantively, inspect representative abstracts,
compare alternative resolutions and preprocessing choices, and assess
stability across fits. Keyword concentration, coherence, and geometric
membership are complementary diagnostics; none alone establishes that
the clusters are the research field's underlying topics.

Algorithms*. Plenum.

word frequency and exclusivity. *Proceedings of the 29th International

extraction. *Proceedings of GSCL*, 31-40.

TF-IDF procedure. arXiv:2203.05794.

Automatically evaluating topic coherence and topic model quality.
*Proceedings of the 14th Conference of the European Chapter of the
Association for Computational Linguistics*, 530-539.

Roberts, M. E., Stewart, B. M., & Tingley, D. (2019). stm: An R package for
